title: Why We Said ‘No’ to IVF and ‘Yes’ to Embryo Adoption
author: Anna Russell
summary: Anna Russell, a seminary-trained mother, recounts how she and her husband navigated unexplained infertility and why they declined IVF in favor of embryo adoption. She explains that research she did in seminary on assisted reproductive technologies left her intellectually prepared but not emotionally or spiritually ready for the grief of repeated disappointment, and she situates her story in figures on how common infertility and IVF have become. The core argument is ethical: if a unique human life begins at fertilization, then destroying or indefinitely freezing surplus embryos, and discarding embryos after genetic testing, is as wrong outside the womb as inside it. Russell is careful to affirm the full dignity of children conceived through IVF and to note where Christians might disagree in good faith. She presents embryo adoption as a redemptive alternative that creates no new embryos, gives existing ones a chance at life, is cheaper and less physically demanding, and allows mothers to carry and nurse their children, while candidly listing its risks, including success rates around 43 to 45 percent and complex origin questions. She closes with practical steps for couples considering it and a reflection on suffering redeemed through the two adopted embryos who became her daughters.
points: Russell's objection to IVF rests on its standard practice of creating multiple embryos, freezing or destroying unused ones, and screening out embryos with likely genetic disorders.
She explicitly distinguishes the ethics of the procedure from the value of children conceived through it, who remain image-bearers regardless of how they were conceived.
Embryo adoption is framed as redemptive because it creates no new embryos and gives some of the roughly 1.2 million frozen US embryos a chance to live within a family.
She is candid about limits: donor embryo transfers succeed only about 43 to 45 percent of the time, and adopted children may struggle with questions about genetic parents.
Her practical counsel for couples is to pray, seek pastoral and peer counsel, ask one's current clinic about embryo adoption, and consider dedicated Christian embryo adoption services.
quotes: By God’s grace, in 2019 I spent hours during our last year of seminary researching and writing about infertility, assisted reproductive technologies, and the ethical issues surrounding their use. At the time, I thought of this as my latest theological hobbyhorse. It was interesting and important to me, but it wasn’t personal.

For those with children or loved ones conceived via IVF, these critiques feel deeply personal. Yet I want to make clear that critiques of IVF have nothing to do with the value and dignity of children conceived via IVF.

If pro-life Christians agree that a unique human life begins at fertilization, then just as early-term abortion that kills an embryo inside the womb is wrong, destroying embryos developed outside the womb is wrong. If couples who conceive naturally shouldn’t abort a pregnancy because the baby has a genetic disorder, then embryos created via IVF shouldn’t be destroyed for the same reason.
Unlike in IVF, no new children are created through embryo adoption. Rather, a child who already exists gets a chance to live and be part of a family.

It’s possible to lament the broken circumstances that led to the child’s need for adoption while also rejoicing in the gift of becoming that child’s parents—as parents of traditionally adopted children do.

The average success rate for a donor embryo transfer is between 43 percent and 45 percent, a discouraging prospect. We’re so grateful that our first embryo transfer led to the healthy birth of our daughter, but we were mentally prepared for the prospect of multiple failed transfers.

As with traditional adoption, these children are likely to have confusing feelings about their origin stories and questions about their genetic parents that may be difficult or impossible for their adoptive parents to answer.
Infertility taught me that protection from suffering isn’t guaranteed in the Christian life. In fact, suffering with and for Jesus is promised.
